## Today's Agenda

- One finding, three explanations
- What a theory is, and what the lens metaphor means
- Three paradigms, and grand versus middle-range theory
- A catalogue of six middle-range theories
- Two lenses on four real chat messages
- Four methods, and why this course uses content analysis

## What You Leave With Today

- Theory sounds like the least useful part of this course, and it decides the most
- Theory tells you which of the thousands of messages in front of you are worth counting
- You leave today with a lens picked for your own project
- You also leave with a reason for picking it that you could say out loud to somebody who disagreed

## One Finding, Three Explanations

Livestream viewing looks more socially motivated than content motivated. Three theories
explain that differently:

- **Uses and gratifications** (Katz, Blumler, & Gurevitch, 1973): viewers are active agents meeting a social need that a finished video cannot
- **Parasocial interaction** (Horton & Wohl, 1956): viewers form one-sided bonds with the streamer, and connection is how that bond feels
- **Social identity** (Tajfel & Turner, 1979): the community is a group, and chat is a space of belonging

The same pattern, under three research programs, becomes three different studies.

## Theory Is Not Speculation

- In casual use "theory" means a guess. In research it means the opposite of a guess
- A **theory** is a formal, systematic explanation of relationships between concepts
- A good theory is **logically coherent**: its parts fit together without contradiction
- It is **generalizable**: it applies across contexts rather than to one case
- It is **falsifiable**: it makes predictions that could turn out wrong
- It is **generative**: it produces new hypotheses rather than closing the question

## Social Identity, Worked

People take part of their self-concept from the groups they belong to (Tajfel & Turner,
1979). That one idea produces three checkable predictions:

- Viewers rate their preferred community above rivals, especially on subjective dimensions like authenticity
- Criticize a streamer and the regulars respond defensively
- In a different domain entirely, partisans rate aligned news outlets as more credible even when the factual content is identical

## The Lens Metaphor

- Theory works like a camera lens: some things come into sharp focus, and some fall outside the frame
- **Appraisal theory** focuses you on individual evaluation, so you build surveys and experiments measuring personal reactions
- **Social identity** focuses you on group meaning, so you analyze how members talk about the stream as a marker of who they are
- The same phenomenon gets different designs, and **neither one is wrong**
- You cannot use every lens at once. Trying produces blur, not depth

## Three Paradigms

- **Social scientific:** an objective reality can be observed and measured
    - The work is deductive: you start from theory and test. It asks *does X cause Y?*
- **Interpretive:** reality is built through interaction
    - The work is inductive: you observe and build theory from what you find. It asks *what does X mean to the people who live it?*
    - Its methods include grounded theory and thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006)
- **Critical and cultural:** power shapes what counts as knowledge
    - It asks *whose interests does X serve, and whose voices go unheard?*

## Grand and Middle-Range Theories

- **Grand theories** explain human behavior across every context: Marxism, psychoanalysis, and structuralism
    - They are intellectually powerful and close to untestable, because the scope is too wide and the predictions too general to be proven wrong
- **Middle-range theories** are specific enough to generate testable hypotheses and broad enough to travel past one case
    - Robert Merton named the zone, and every theory in the catalogue ahead sits in it

## Catalogue: Relationship and Group Theories

- **Parasocial interaction** (Horton & Wohl, 1956) is one-sided bonds with media figures that feel intimate but are not reciprocated
    - It predicts stronger connection with more consumption, and a sense of betrayal when a scandal breaks
    - It is the lens for donations to strangers and for influencer marketing
- **Social identity** (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) says group membership shapes self-concept
    - It predicts in-group favoritism and symbolic boundary keeping
    - It is foundational in political communication and sports fandom

## Catalogue: Media and Message Theories

- **Agenda setting** (McCombs & Shaw, 1972) says media do not tell people what to think, but they tell people what to think about
    - On Twitch the front page, the recommendations, and the category rankings all set an agenda
- **Framing** (Goffman, 1974; Entman, 1993) says how information is presented shapes how it is read
    - Episodic framing pushes blame toward individuals, and thematic framing pushes it toward structures
    - You can see framing in how streamers title their own broadcasts

## Catalogue: Audience and Exposure Theories

- **Uses and gratifications** (Katz, Blumler, & Gurevitch, 1973) says audiences are active and pick media to meet needs
    - It is the lens behind most research on why people watch other people play video games (Sjöblom & Hamari, 2017)
- **Cultivation** (Gerbner & Gross, 1976) says long-term cumulative exposure shapes how people perceive social reality
    - Heavy consumers overestimate what they keep seeing, most strongly where they have no direct experience to check it against

## Two Lenses on the Same Chat

Here are four messages from one Twitch broadcast. Read them once before we put a lens on
them:

> **DragoBoi89:** xQc actually playing well today wtf
>
> **emotelord:** PogU PogU
>
> **realnamedfan:** @xqcow do u remember when u said hi to me last week
>
> **streamfan22:** chat is this real

## Two Readings of Those Messages

- **Uses and gratifications** sees four needs and four viewers: evaluative commentary, collective emotional expression, direct acknowledgment, and collective sense-making
    - All four messages are equally interesting to this lens
- **Parasocial interaction** sees realnamedfan as the case
    - An @-address plus a memory claim about a previous acknowledgment treats a one-sided interaction as a continuing relationship
    - emotelord and streamfan22 never address the streamer, so this lens pushes them to the edges
- The same four messages make two different studies

## Four Methods, Four Questions

- **Surveys** measure what people report. They are natural for uses and gratifications, and limited by the gap between what people say and what they do
- **Experiments** isolate cause by manipulating something. They are natural for "does X cause Y?", and limited by artificiality
- **Qualitative methods** capture meaning and lived experience. They are natural for the interpretive question, and they trade breadth for depth
- **Content analysis** quantifies features of the content itself, at a scale nobody could eyeball

## Why Content Analysis Here

This course uses content analysis for three reasons, and none of them is that it is the
best method:

- **Fit:** the shared example data *is* content, millions of messages and stream records
- **Pedagogical completeness:** you practice operationalization, sampling, reliability, and analysis on one dataset, without recruiting a single human subject
- **Transfer:** a precise codebook, tested reliability, and systematic sampling are what make every other method work too

Choosing a method with the alternatives in view beats choosing by default.
